title-group.article-title: The shadow of mercury behind gold extraction in the Amazon: hidden threats to human health and the environment

body.p: The price of gold is rising exponentially, reaching a value of up to 5000 USD per ounce in recent months, while it was only 1072 USD in 2015 due to international economic uncertainty. The World Gold Council estimates that 8.5% of the global gold production between 2014 and 2024 was provided by the Amazon region through informal/illegal mining.1 The environmental consequences of this activity are devastating, since dangerous substances such as mercury and cyanide are used for gold extraction. It is estimated that for every kilogram of gold extracted, up to 5 kg of mercury are discarded into the environment, thus contaminating water sources and threatening people's health.

The United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) estimated that artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) accounted for 38% of global mercury aerial emissions in 2015 (approximately 838 tons of mercury).2 According to the same report, more than 70% of South America's total mercury emissions into the air come from ASGM. UNEP also estimated that ASGM releases an average of 1220 tonnes of mercury per year in soil and water. Therefore, mercury illegally used for gold extraction in the Amazon represents a hidden threat in addition to air pollutants recently described by Jaramillo-Aguilar et al. on this journal,3 as well as a potential contaminant for food chain, to be considered in the frame of food-environment policies in Latin America.4 There is already evidence of mercury-related health damages in Amazonian populations, particularly on nervous system, and specifically on movements and sight.5,6 Some studies also suggest that exposure to mercury derived from mining in pregnant women may cause cognitive delays in the foetus.7

Last year, 11 soldiers were killed in the Ecuadorian province of Orellana during an operation against illegal mining. This event reflects that illegal mining not only generates violence and crime but also expresses poverty, state of abandonment, and the destruction of indigenous and peasant territories. More than 60% of the Ecuadorian Amazon is concessioned for mining activities, sometimes over indigenous territories, without guaranteeing the safety of water sources. Even legal mining operations can be used to “launder” gold extracted illegally and informally. According to the NGO “Human Rights Watch”, violence in the Amazon has skyrocketed and now exceeds the regional average in Latin America.8 In just one year, murders increased by more than 200% in the Ecuadorian provinces of Zamora, Morona, and Orellana, where in some municipalities they exceed 400%. Territorial defenders are criminalized or killed, and have been subjected to threats, assaults, and persecution for their work denouncing and resisting the expansion of illegal mining and environmental contamination. The Ecuadorian Amazon is one of the most well-documented settings for systematic violence against people defending the land and the environment. COICA (Coordinating Body of Indigenous Organisations of the Amazon Basin) warns that 358 Indigenous activists were killed in the Amazon in 2021.9 In a 2024 report led by NGO “Global Witness”, 117 of the 146 murders or disappearances of environmental defenders documented worldwide occurred in Latin America.10 Only in Ecuador, the “Alianza de Organizaciones por los Derechos Humanos” documented 449 acts of intimidations between 2011 and 2021, while the government officially computed 5 murders of human rights defenders between 2013 and 2022. Even the Pan-Amazonian Ecclesial Network in Ecuador (REPAM) has firmly denounced irresponsible mining exploitation and contamination affecting the Amazon. It has been highlighted how illegal mining poisons rivers with heavy metals and destroys the jungle without respecting basic ecological norms.

What activists are demanding is the full traceability of gold in international markets, stopping mining concessions in Amazon Indigenous territories, strengthening legal and personal protection for environmental defenders, and promoting policies that repair and bring environmental justice. This would not only stop illegal gold extraction causing environmental destruction and threats to human health, but will also reduce violence and social disintegration.
